prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its identification as an incretin hormone, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots placed GLP-1 first, and I do not treat that unanimity as evidence in itself. The case rests on the science. It is a clear physiological discovery: a gut hormone that amplifies glucose-dependent insulin secretion and acts on appetite and gastric emptying. It was followed by decades of independent confirmation, and the physiology led directly to drugs with large effects on diabetes, obesity and, in randomized outcome trials, cardiovascular and renal disease. The discovery, its clinical consequence and its maturity are all established, so the Prize would be recognizing a finished arc rather than a promise. A trio of Holst (native peptide physiology and processing), Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology, the therapeutic rationale) and Mojsov (the active truncated peptide) credits the physiological discovery, which is what the Prize is meant to reward, and keeps the drug-development story as its consequence.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. The three-person limit forces us to leave out Knudsen, whose long-acting acylated analogues are what turned the physiology into a medicine used by millions, and Habener, whose proglucagon and GLP-1 work is not among the credited names. Mojsov's priority relative to other early contributors is disputed. A prize built on physiology risks being read as ignoring the drug that changed practice, and a prize built on drug development risks ignoring the physiology. Long-term safety and durability of effect are also still accumulating.

responses.point: Sandberg proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen rather than Mojsov, arguing that the arc from physiology to long-acting analogue design is what makes the discovery transformative and that Knudsen covers the therapeutic end.
responses.response: I take the point that the medicine exists because of Knudsen's work, and I do not dismiss it. But I still prefer Mojsov to Knudsen. The Prize is for the discovery, and Mojsov's identification of the biologically active truncated GLP-1 is what made the peptide a viable physiological and therapeutic target. Knudsen's work is an outstanding feat of pharmaceutical optimization of a mechanism that already existed. I would give up this preference only if the committee decides that the citation should explicitly cover the translation into drugs, in which case Knudsen should replace Mojsov, because a four-name arc cannot be squeezed into three. I would like to hear whether anyone considers the Mojsov priority question settled.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked optogenetics third with Bamberg, Nagel and Hegemann, saying the channelrhodopsin discovery is the decisive step and that excluding Boyden, Deisseroth and Miesenböck would be contentious.
responses.response: I partly agree and partly disagree. Channelrhodopsin as a light-gated channel is the original, decisive discovery, and I agree that a set without Bamberg is hard to defend. But my opening trio of Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann was an attempt to cover both the molecular discovery and the neuronal demonstration in three names. If we cannot find a configuration that excludes none of Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth and Miesenböck without a serious injustice, I now think that is a reason not to put optogenetics at the top this year, not a reason to pick any trio. It remains a strong alternative, but its attribution is harder than that of GLP-1. Optogenetics also has less direct clinical impact, though it is a very important tool for circuit neuroscience, my own field.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked CAR-T second with only June and Sadelain, judging Rosenberg's decisive contribution to be adoptive T-cell therapy rather than the engineered-receptor discovery.
responses.response: I agree with this and I now think I was wrong to include Rosenberg in my opening CAR-T trio. Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy and TIL work is foundational but is a distinct line of discovery, and including him blurs the citation. June and Sadelain is the cleaner pair, though Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept remains a fairness problem that no pair solves. CAR-T is therefore my first alternative. I still place it below GLP-1 because the cure rate in solid tumours is low and the toxicity profile is still evolving, whereas GLP-1 has established, broad and sustained benefit.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked HPV vaccines seventh, noting very strong population-level effectiveness data, but also that the 2008 prize for the HPV and cervical cancer link, together with Zhou's early death and parallel commercial development, complicates attribution.
responses.response: I agree that the effectiveness data are now compelling and that HPV vaccination is a real public-health achievement. The attribution problem you describe is substantial, since one of the central contributors cannot be honoured and priority between the NCI and Frazer groups is contested, so I do not see it as a leading candidate this year. I do not hold that the 2008 prize disqualifies it, because the vaccine is a different achievement from the causal link. I would want to see a clear and defensible three-name split before supporting it.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority claim is settled well enough to justify her place over Knudsen or Habener in the trio.
Whether the citation should recognize physiology only or physiology and drug development, which determines whether Knudsen should be a laureate.
Whether a clean three-name optogenetics configuration exists that does not exclude a central contributor.
Long-term safety and durability of GLP-1 therapy, which are still accumulating, though they do not seem to me to affect the case for the discovery itself.
I am relying on my own recollection of the field history and have not independently verified the priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates from my provided profile. My documented connections (a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, work with Patrik Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann) do not involve any credited candidate. I work in motor circuits, so I have an interest in optogenetics as a tool but no documented personal tie to any of its credited names.
